May the Beacon hold.

The Umbra

What Every Venturer Needs to Know

The following is adapted from "A Treatise on the Breath of the Void" by Scholar Ehre of House Thalum — required reading for all Explorers' Guild initiates before first descent.

What It Is

The Umbra is not mere darkness. It is an ancient, sentient miasma — a hive-minded shroud of indigo-black that moves through the lowest places of the world like a drowning tide. It was not always present. Before the Apostasy, the natural cycle of life, death, and divine maintenance held it in check. When the gods departed, those mechanisms failed. The Umbra expanded to fill the void they left.

It manifests as a clinging liquid darkness that settles into lowlands, ravines, and the spaces beneath things. Only altitude and the Beacon's light push it back. Outside the plateau, it is everywhere. In the Wastes, the air itself is its territory.

What It Does to the Living

Prolonged exposure to the Umbra induces Flesh-Discord — a slow, agonizing transformation of the natural form. Scholars have identified three stages:

The Blight — The earliest signs: a sickness of the marrow, skin beginning to shed, a ghastly translucency spreading beneath the surface. At this stage, withdrawal to clean air and Beacon light can halt progression.

The Warp — The budding of extra sensory organs, jagged bone-spurs breaking through skin, a sickly violet ichor replacing blood in the veins. Reversal at this stage is possible but difficult, requiring significant Caretaker intervention.

Unnatural Melding — In the deepest concentrations of heavy Umbra, the resonance can fuse distinct living things into a single, agonized mass of flesh and shadow. No recorded reversal exists.

The Umbra Hungers for Magic

The Umbra is not indiscriminate — it gravitates toward magical beings and magical expression. The greater the arcane potency, the faster it comes. During the collapse following the Apostasy, the most powerful wizards were consumed first. Dragons, beings of inherent magical nature, suffered the same fate.

As a practical matter: the more actively you channel magic in the Wastes, the more attention you draw. This is not a reason not to use magic. It is a reason to be deliberate about when and how.

The Malignant Echo

The Umbra emits a constant low vibration — a Malignant Echo — that pierces stone and skin alike. It is felt more than heard: a rot-heavy chime at the edge of perception that unravels the spirit over time. Extended exposure without protection degrades focus, memory, and eventually coherent thought.

This is not metaphor. The Echo is measurable. Experienced Slayers can identify the type and approximate size of an Umbra-touched creature simply by the specific frequency of the Echo it emits.

The Hollowing

The full subversion of a mind to the Umbra is called Hollowing. It is total.

  1. Memory-Sifting — The Echo shatters the mind's history. The victim begins to lose personal memories: faces, names, the reasons they started doing things.
  2. Extinction — The personality dissolves. The vital spark dies. The body becomes a necrotic vessel.
  3. The Revenant — The shell reanimates with unnatural strength and cold, instinctive cunning. It remembers nothing of who it was, but it retains every combat reflex, every skill, every ingrained pattern of movement. A Hollowed soldier still fights like a soldier. A Hollowed mage still casts.

Arch-Revenants are the category that keeps experienced Slayers awake at night: former Venturers or powerful individuals whose Hollowing preserved their full capabilities — magic, tactics, combat skill — while erasing everything human about them. They act as generals, organizing lesser Umbra-touched into coordinated forces with a discipline that should be impossible for beings with no consciousness. They are not thinking. They are performing — executing the patterns of a lifetime's training on an empty stage. Reports suggest organized Arch-Revenant commands are converging on the plateau.

Memory-Bargains

In extremis, Venturers have survived deep Umbra exposure through Memory-Bargains — sacrificing personal memories to the Umbra's resonance in order to avoid full Hollowing. The sacrifice buys time and distance. It does not cure the exposure. The memories do not return.

Some Venturers have returned from the Wastes missing years of their lives — unable to recognize family members, carrying grief they cannot explain because they no longer remember why they are sad. Grand Explorer Mira Ravenna is the Vale's most prominent practitioner. She has forgotten the face of her own child, and she carries this with a sharp, dark humor that fools nobody.

Surviving It

The Beacon's light is the primary defense. The plateau is clean. The closer to Medsen's centre, the stronger the ward.

Ashlines — paint mixed with Beacon ash, applied to walls and structures — generate a passive ward. Emberfort's rebuilt walls are treated. Checkpoint outpost perimeters are maintained with Ashlines.

Lumen Censers — portable vessels of distilled Beacon light — provide limited but life-saving protection in the field. Standard equipment for Venturing parties.

The Embermark — a ritual burn left on Emberguard members by the Beacon's Cold-Flame — provides minor resistance to the Malignant Echo. Slayers develop a more robust version through the Ingress of Ash.

Altitude helps. The Umbra settles low. Staying above treeline reduces exposure, though it does not eliminate it.

The Creatures It Creates

Beyond the Hollowed, the Umbra shapes the natural world into something worse.

The Wastes' flora and fauna mutate under the Umbra's hive influence. Trees become brittle black glass or weeping resonators that broadcast the Echo. Animals lose their original forms, merging into nightmarish multi-limbed predators.

Rotlords — massive, mobile ecosystems of rotting flesh and fungal growth, constantly expanding, amplifying the Malignant Echo to warp all life in their vicinity. The Slayers hunt them. It is not easy work.

Shatter-Wing Angels — blasphemous, corrupted remnants of forgotten divine beings. They serve as heralds of the void, their original sacred purpose inverted into something that cannot be named without discomfort.

Umbra-Touched Fiends — corrupted extraplanar entities trapped in the Wastes since the Apostasy. They retain their infernal instincts and considerable power.

Dragons — believed extinct as a species. What remains are massive Umbra-touched mutations in the deepest Wastes. The Aetherweaver Academy reportedly holds the last safe eggs in stasis. What a dragon becomes when fully Hollowed is one of the Vale's most feared theoretical scenarios, and one that several scholars believe is no longer theoretical.

A History of the Enduring

Legendarium & Timeline of Brightvale

Part One — The Legendarium

Key terms every resident of Brightvale knows. Newcomers who get these wrong are usually from somewhere they shouldn't be.

The Apostasy — The catastrophe. Roughly four hundred years ago, the gods departed without explanation. The crimson veil sealed the sky. The Umbra was unleashed. The Armisian Empire collapsed in months. The Apostasy is year zero — all dates are measured from it.

After Apostasy (AA) — The calendar. The current year is 400 AA.

The Armisian Empire — The great human civilization that dominated the world before the Apostasy. Its ruins, relics, and secrets fill the Wastes. The Noble Houses are its surviving aristocracy.

The Enduring — The collective name for all peoples who survived the Apostasy and built Brightvale. A term of identity and defiance, not a specific ancestry.

Brightvale — The protected plateau in the Teardrop Mountains. The last confirmed safe habitation in the known world.

The Beacon — The pillar of holy fire at the heart of Medsen, ignited by the Dawnfather's sacrifice. It keeps the plateau clear of Umbra. It is slowly dimming.

The Dawnfather — The martyr who sacrificed his soul to create the Beacon at the Apostasy's darkest hour. The Sun-Born monarchy claims descent from him.

The Umbra — The sentient, parasitic darkness that fills the world beyond the plateau. (See: The Umbra)

The Wastes / The Wilds — Everything outside Brightvale's walls. Umbra-choked, geographically unstable, and full of things that once were not dangerous.

Revenant — A person fully Hollowed by the Umbra: dead inside, reanimated as an Umbra-driven shell. They retain muscle memory and instinct but not self.

Arch-Revenant — A Revenant who retained extraordinary capability — magic, tactics, leadership — through the Hollowing. The most dangerous class of Umbra threat.

Hollowing — The full subversion of a soul by the Umbra. Total erasure of self.

The Warping of Flesh — The physical mutation caused by prolonged Umbra exposure. Ranges from skin-shedding to complete bodily transformation.

Ashgeld — The standard currency. Coins pressed from Beacon ash; warm to the touch, faintly luminous in total darkness. Stable, backed by the most reliable institution in the Vale.

Lumen — Distilled Beacon light, infused into wood or stored in Censers. Used to push back the Umbra in the field. Produced by the Aetherweaver Academy.

Venturers — Those who descend into the Wastes on expedition. Not soldiers, not scholars, not saints — usually a mixture of all three.

The Venturer's Trail — The primary mountain pass descending from the plateau into the Wastes, guarded at its head by Emberfort.

Ashlines — Beacon ash mixed into paint, applied to fortifications, armour and shields to generate passive Umbra wards.

Sun-Born — The royal bloodline, claiming divine descent from the Dawnfather. The current king, Alfwyn, is Sun-Born — or claims to be.

The Brightblood War — The civil war (293–297 AA) that nearly destroyed Brightvale from the inside. A wound the Vale has not finished healing.

Embermark — The silvery-gray ritual mark burned into some Emberguard members by the Beacon's Flame. Some people are born with it.

Part Two — A History of the Enduring

The official timeline as maintained by the scribes of Medsen. What is not recorded here is considered lost. Depending on how knowledgeable your character is, you may be more or less familiar with the older details.

Year 0 — The Apostasy

The gods departed. The crimson veil sealed the sky. The Umbra consumed civilization. The Armisian Empire, which had stood for centuries, collapsed within months. Dragons fell. Cities burned. The few who survived began to walk north.

~Year 5 — The Sacrifice and the Beacon

A man history calls the Dawnfather gave his soul to ignite the Beacon on the Teardrop plateau. Survivors established the first settlement at Medsen in the Beacon's light. It was a refugee camp. It became a city.

Year 25 — Hvergi Founded

Dwarven refugees consolidated in the eastern peaks, founding Hvergi and beginning the deep-seam mines that still power Brightvale's industry.

Year ~87 — The Seared Oracles (disputed)

A sect of Beacon followers was condemned by the early Caretakers for uncovering something the authorities would not name. The sect was sealed alive in a vault beneath the Dawnfather Temple. Official records on the matter were destroyed. Caretaker orthodoxy teaches that the sect fell to heresy. The specifics remain deliberately struck from the archive.

Year 164 — The First Archive

Arch-Mage Elowen the Wise — First Steward of the early Medsen government — ordered formal recording of all surviving history after scholars noticed the memory-eroding effects of Umbra exposure on the population.

Years 168–284 — The Age of Cynred the Bitter

King Cynred ruled for 116 years through deliberate isolation and institutional neglect. He closed borders to survivors, refused audiences, and allowed Brightvale to calcify. When he died, his grandson King Aldhelm inherited a structurally intact realm with a politically poisoned court.

Year 252 — The Slayers' Guild Founded

Lord Eadmer, the "Paragon of Steel," organized elite monster hunters following the first major breach of Emberfort's South Palisades.

Year 270 — The Scholastic Schism

First Steward Elowen resigned following a bitter dispute over "Deep-Weave" scholarship — the recovery and study of pre-Apostasy human magic. The dispute split the scholarly community and directly led to the Academy's refounding.

Year 271 — The Aetherweaver Academy Founded

The Scholars' Guild rebranded as the Aetherweaver Academy, relocating to the cliffs of Aurore's Peak and committing to teaching Aetherweaving to all capable initiates.

Years 293–297 — The Brightblood War

Civil war between the Crown's Coalition and a Reform Coalition of Noble Houses. Four years of urban combat in Medsen, ending when the Beacon flickered, Emberfort fell to a Hollowed general named Lord-Warden Theron, and both sides were forced to unite against the Horde at Three Bridges. King Aldhelm died there, his Sun-Born radiance burning through the Horde and through himself. The war is considered Brightvale's deepest wound. The sides, technically, are still remembered.

Years 297–308 — The Golden Reprieve

Queen Wendreda pardoned lesser rebels and sacrificed the most dangerous Reform leaders to the Beacon. A decade of recovery produced Ashlines, Lumen Censers, and the Warding Expansion that doubled Medsen's safe living zone.

Year 329 — The Explorers' Guild Founded

King Oswin "The Venturer" formalized expeditions into the Wastes. The Guild was born.

Years 354–356 — The Great Famine

Three years of crop failure under King Raedfryd's mismanagement. Ended when Raedfryd sacrificed himself to the Beacon's Great Pyre. The people did not grieve publicly.

Year 357 — The Council of Seven Formed

In the wake of the royal self-sacrifice, the Council was established to permanently check the monarchy's authority. The crown became ceremonial.

Year 385 — Mira Ravenna Becomes Grand Explorer

The current leader of the Explorers' Guild assumes command following the death of Grand Explorer Lorenzo.

Year 393 — The Silent Sovereignty

King Alfwyn is crowned and almost immediately retreats into the Central Temple-Castle, ceasing all public appearances. He has not been seen in seven years. The High Steward speaks in his name.

Year 399 — The Southern Quake

A massive earthquake reshapes the southern Wastes. New routes are opened. Old ones are buried. What the quake disturbed in the deep lowlands is not yet known.

Year 400 — Discovery of the Chasm

Now. Landslides from the quake's aftermath have revealed multiple entrances to The Chasm — an ancient underground complex beneath the plateau itself. No map of the interior yet exists. Origin unknown. Explorers' Guild expeditions are ongoing.

The Order of Brightvale

Government, Institutions, and Faith

The Council of Seven

Brightvale is nominally a monarchy. In practice, it is governed by the Council of Seven — a body established in 357 AA after the last absolute king immolated himself into the Beacon to end a famine he had caused. The Enduring decided, collectively, that one person should probably not hold that much power again.

The Council consists of seven seats:

The Five Permanent Seats

These are held by the leaders of the Vale's core institutions. Their authority does not depend on elections — they hold their seats as long as they hold their positions.

SeatHolderRepresents
High CaretakerKaelen (Infernis)The Caretakers of the Beacon; religious doctrine; preservation of the Light
Lord Commander of the EmberguardVaris Lugner (Infernis)Internal military order; civil law; defense of settlements
Arch Aetherweaver(current holder not public)The Academy; arcane research; Brightvale's intellectual future
First SlayerMakjar One-Eyed (Orc)The Slayers; the war against the Umbra; Waste expertise
Grand ExplorerMira RavennaThe Explorers' Guild; outward expansion; Waste reclamation

The Two Rotating Noble Seats

These seats are occupied by Noble House representatives elected every two years. In theory, this gives the aristocracy a voice in governance. In practice, the five permanent factions collude aggressively during election cycles, backing allied Houses to secure proxy votes at the Council table. The Noble elections are, functionally, a proxy war between the Guilds. The aristocracy knows this and considers it the cost of relevance.

The Monarchy

The royal family claims to be the Sun-Born — direct descendants of the Dawnfather himself. For centuries, this claim was backed by a visible, demonstrable ability to channel radiant holy light, which made it difficult to dispute openly.

The monarchy's absolute power ended following generations of mismanagement: famines, border closures, a civil war that nearly destroyed the Vale. Today, the King retains a ceremonial seat on the Council and the symbolic weight of the Dawnfather's legacy. Real authority rests with the Council.

King Alfwyn, the current sovereign, has not been seen publicly in seven years. He withdrew into the Central Temple-Castle — built directly over the Beacon's heart — and ceased all public appearances shortly after his coronation. The High Steward manages the crown's administrative duties and holds his Council seat as proxy. Theories about the King's condition are, at this point, a cottage industry in every common room in Medsen.

The Guilds and the Houses

The fundamental tension of Brightvale's politics is between the five Guilds (which hold actual resources and practical power) and the Noble Houses (which hold historical legitimacy and land rights inherited from the Armisian Empire).

The Houses maintain feudal claims over surrounding lands, forts, and fiefs. They fund institutions, back Council candidates, forge alliances, and conduct proxy wars through commerce and election cycles. They are powerful.

The Guilds, however, control the things people cannot live without: the Beacon's maintenance, the walls' defense, monster culling, Waste mapping, and arcane research. In a crisis, the Guild that holds Emberfort's garrison matters more than the House that owns the farmland behind it.

This tension is not resolved. It is managed, imperfectly, season by season.

The Three Faiths

Religion in Brightvale is inseparable from politics because the Beacon is simultaneously the city's primary theological object and its most important piece of survival infrastructure. Three positions divide the faithful — and the debate shapes every significant decision the Vale makes about its future.

The Orthodoxy

"The Light is divine and must not be touched."

The dominant position, held by the Caretakers and a significant portion of the common population. The Beacon is the literal residue of the Dawnfather's sacrifice — sacred fire, holy beyond mortal comprehension. Its flickering is a divine sign, a response to the failings of the Enduring. To study it, to tamper with it, to treat it as a mechanism rather than a miracle, is blasphemy. The faithful weathered famines with prayer. They will weather the flickering the same way.

The Stoics

"The Light endures, and so must we."

A quieter tradition. The Beacon is sacred, yes — but its fluctuations are not punishments. They are simply the nature of a divine thing existing in an imperfect world. The light waxes and wanes. The faithful do not panic when it dims, and do not claim credit when it brightens. They endure. The name is the prayer. This position is common among veterans, older citizens, and those who have spent time outside the walls — people who have seen enough to know that not everything that hurts is a punishment.

The Pragmatists

"The Light is power, and power must be understood."

Favored by the Academy's progressive scholars and, quietly, several Noble Houses. The Beacon is extraordinary — perhaps the most significant magical artifact in the known world — but it is still an artifact. It was made. It operates on principles that can be studied. If the Beacon can be understood, it can be maintained. If maintained, it can be improved. If improved, the Enduring can stop merely surviving and start reclaiming what was lost. The Orthodoxy considers this heretical. The Pragmatists consider that a secondary concern.

The Economy

Brightvale runs on Ashgeld — coins pressed from Beacon ash, warm to the touch, faintly luminous in complete darkness. The Caretakers control the mint. The currency is considered the most stable in any world that still has one.

The economic geography of the Vale:

  • The Halfling Hearthlands — The agricultural heart. Produces the majority of Brightvale's food through communal agrarian techniques and a regulated supply of Beacon ash fertilizer from Medsen.
  • Hvergi — The industrial heart. Produces nearly all Brightvale's iron, stone, fine crafted goods, and the arcane crystals that supply the Academy's research.
  • Veikryss — The primary timber source. Supplies construction and commercial wood across the region.
  • Emberfort, Three Bridges, Veikryss — The logistics spine. These three settlements are enriched beyond their size by serving as the supply funnel for Venturing expeditions: outfitting departing parties, supporting the checkpoint network, and processing the flow of recovered Waste artifacts into the Guild economy.

The wealthiest private individuals in Brightvale are, in order: the heads of the Guilds, the leading Noble Houses, and the merchants who figured out how to be useful to both.

The Guilds

The Guilds are the spine of the Vale. The Houses own the estate. The Guilds own its survival.

The Caretakers of the Beacon

Order of the Eternal Hearth

The oldest institution in Brightvale — predating the Council, predating the Monarchy in any formal sense, predating nearly everything. The Order of the Eternal Hearth, commonly called the Caretakers, maintains the Beacon. Without them, the holy fire dims. Without the holy fire, everything else is academic.

Their responsibilities extend far beyond the literal flame. The Caretakers perform the Last Rites — the rituals that prevent the dead from rising as Revenants, which is considerably more urgent in Brightvale than in most places. They conduct Awakening Rituals for the Emberborne. They distill the Beacon's light into Lumen-Casks, the portable light-vessels that keep Venturing parties alive in the Wastes. They run Brightvale's most extensive charity network, providing healing and sustenance throughout the city. They are ubiquitous, they are essential, and they ask, in exchange, only that you not question what they do behind closed doors. These are considered spiritual matters.

The Caretakers represent the Orthodox theological position: the Beacon is divine, sacred, and not to be studied or tampered with. This position supports their institutional authority. It is also, they would say, simply correct.

Current Leader: High Caretaker Kaelen, an Infernis of severe bearing and genuine radiance. Kaelen and the Order's senior priests are often partially blind from years of staring into the Beacon's heart. They believe the city survives through divine sacrifice — which, in a sense, is technically true.

Seat: The Dawnfather Temple, Medsen.

The Emberguard

Shield of the Vale

The Emberguard is Brightvale's internal military force: its police, its border patrol, its civil order, and its first response when something comes down from the mountains that shouldn't be there. They are headquartered at Emberfort — the great bastion at the head of the Venturer's Trail — and maintain "Glow-Stations" (smaller outposts) along the valley's major routes and within Medsen itself.

Every Emberguard member undergoes the Ashen Oath: a ritual involving the Beacon's Cold-Flame that leaves a silvery-gray Embermark on their forearms and grants minor resistance to the Umbra's Malignant Echo. Their tactical doctrine is built around tight formations and overlapping defensive auras — the Chain of Flame — designed to create a temporary pocket of Beacon-adjacent protection in the field.

Their roles within the Vale:

  • Border Defense — First line against mountain-dwelling horrors and Umbra-tainted beasts approaching the plateau.
  • Civil Policing — Law enforcement within settlements; enforcement of rations and the "Sanctity of Light."
  • Mobilization — When a threat is detected, they determine whether it requires their rank-and-file, a Slayers contract, or Venturer support.

They are not the Vale's most celebrated institution. But when something goes wrong at three in the morning, they are the ones who show up.

Current Leader: Lord Commander Varis Lugner, an Infernis of House Lugner, recognizable by his gray-blue skin and sweeping dark horns. A veteran of the Crimson-Gloom incursions, credited with modernizing Emberfort's ballista defenses. His strict enforcement of the Common Ration has earned him friction with newer houses. Never seen without his ancestral plate armor, which is said to hum faintly in harmony with the Beacon.

Seat: Emberfort.

The Slayers

Elite of the Wastes

The Slayers are the specialists called when the Emberguard determines that what has come down the mountain requires something beyond soldiers. They hunt the great abominations: Rotlords, Arch-Revenants, Warp-Nests, and things the Wastes produce that don't yet have names. They are, without serious dispute, the most dangerous people in Brightvale.

The Ingress of Ash

Slayer training begins with the Ingress of Ash: controlled exposure to concentrated Umbra-resonance and alchemical mutagens derived from Beacon light. Those who survive emerge with superhuman reflexes, enhanced senses, and a minor immunity to the Umbra's corrupting influence. They are no longer entirely human. They are finely tuned instruments of destruction who also possess an empirical knowledge of the Umbra — its anatomy, its patterns, its weak points — that surpasses anything taught in the Academy's lecture halls.

The Verse of the Blade

The dominant philosophy among current Slayers is the Verse of the Blade — an Orcish tradition that treats combat as high art. Its premise: a warrior who fights without soul is no better than the beasts in the Wastes. Hollowing does not only come from outside. A mind that becomes pure violence eventually loses what makes it worth saving. Expression — in movement, in craftsmanship, in how you choose to face what's trying to kill you — is what keeps the edge sharp on the inside.

This philosophy has spread well beyond Orcish Slayers. It is now the cultural dominant of the entire Guild.

Admission

Joining the Slayers is not a matter of signing a ledger or passing a sparring test. A candidate must Venture into the Wastes at least once and return with a new piece of knowledge about the Umbra-touched — something the Guild does not already know. Hearsay is not sufficient; the knowledge must be specific, firsthand, and actionable. The candidate then presents their findings to assembled Slayers at The Pit in Emberfort, who vote on whether the candidate demonstrates the quality of mind the Guild demands. Surviving the Wastes matters. Knowing what you saw there matters more.

Current Leader: First Slayer Makjar One-Eyed, an Orc who lost her eye during a calculated sacrifice in a three-day pursuit of a Rotblood. Foremost master of the Verse of the Blade. Considers keeping warriors' souls sharp to be as important as keeping their blades so.

"The Scholars talk of the Umbra as a darkness to be feared. We know it as a beast to be bled. You can't understand the Void until you've tasted its ichor on your blade."

Seat: Emberfort (The Pit).

The Explorers' Guild

Trailblazers of the End-Times

The Explorers' Guild serves as the administrative backbone for all expeditions into the Wastes. While Venturers belong to many different guilds—Slayers, Caretakers, Aetherweavers, and even Emberguards—it is the Explorers' Guild that sets the task boards, maintains the checkpoint network, records the maps, and pushes the Council to be more aggressive about reclaiming what was lost. They are obsessed with the past — the ruins, the relics, and the buried knowledge of the Armisian Empire — and with the possibility that the world beyond the valley might, someday, be survivable again.

What They Do

  • Waste Mapping — The geography of the Wastes shifts constantly under Umbra-flux and lingering spell-scars. Keeping accurate maps is a survival matter for every expedition that follows.
  • Checkpoint Establishment — They build and maintain magically-shielded outposts in the Wastes where parties can rest, resupply, and find emergency supplies. Expanding the checkpoint network is a standing priority.
  • Artifact Recovery — Pre-Apostasy relics are the Guild's primary funding source and the Academy's primary research material. Bringing them back is core business.
  • Mountain Surveillance — They monitor and map the Teardrop Mountain passes, ensuring glaciers remain impassable to Umbra-touched and searching for routes into uncharted regions.

Technical Routes

The Guild maintains tight records on Technical Routes through the mountains' sheer faces — paths too demanding for the mindless Umbra-touched to navigate. These "Brave-Paths" allow elite Venturers to enter the Wastes from unexpected angles. They are the Guild's most closely guarded operational secrets.

Culture

The Guild has the highest mortality rate of any institution in Brightvale. This produces a certain kind of personality: rowdy, charismatic, fatalistic, and deeply loyal to the people who chose to walk into the same dark places. The Guild-Hall at Emberfort is the warmest building in the coldest profession.

Current Leader: Grand Explorer Mira Ravenna, a veteran whose name is synonymous with gambling on survival and winning. She has participated in Memory-Bargains to survive Umbra exposures that should have Hollowed her, losing significant personal memories — including the face of her own child — in exchange for returning to lead her people. She carries this with a sharp, dark humor that fools nobody who looks closely.

"The Wastes don't just take your life. They take your Tuesday afternoons and your first kiss, too. At least I've forgotten why I'm supposed to be sad."

Seat: Emberfort (the Guild-Hall).

The Aetherweaver Academy

The Light Was Made — What Was Made Can Be Understood

The Academy sits carved into the cliffs of Aurore's Peak: a sprawling complex of cobalt stone and silver-veined marble, tiered balconies overlooking the central valley, ozone-scented laboratories where the Vale's mages are trained, and a Tower at the summit housing the Arch-Aetherweavers and a grand multi-lensed observatory for reading the winter Auroras.

The Academy teaches Aetherweaving — structured, formulaic arcane magic — to all capable initiates regardless of ancestry. It also houses the Vale's primary arcane research operation: ward reinforcement, Lumen production, and the enduring effort to understand what the Beacon actually is and how it actually works.

Two Patrons, One Battlefield

The Academy is the site of the Vale's most significant ongoing ideological conflict, funded from opposite directions by two noble houses.

House Lugner backs the Old Magic faction — scholars working to recover the pre-Apostasy human tradition of instinct-based, unstructured magic. Their premise: the Armisian Deep-Weaves were not what caused the Apostasy. Their loss was. Recovering them is the path forward.

House Von Zoltraak backs the Progressive Aetherweaving faction — scholars who argue that new arcane forms, developed in direct response to current conditions, are categorically more useful than reviving a tradition that failed to prevent the Apostasy in the first place.

Individual scholars spend considerable energy trying to secure grants from both factions without antagonizing either. A growing number have simply relocated to the Crucible — Von Zoltraak's independent laboratory complex at Aurore's mid-tier — to avoid the politics entirely. The Arch-Aetherweavers of the Tower maintain public neutrality, which satisfies no one.

Seat: Aurore's Peak (main campus); the Crucible (Aurore mid-tier, independent labs).

The Noble Houses

"The Houses are the Empire's echo — the part that survived by being useful."

The Noble Houses are the remnants of the Armisian Empire's aristocracy. Some trace their lineages to before the Apostasy. Others were elevated afterward for services rendered during the collapse. Together, they form the feudal backbone of Brightvale's social order — holding land rights, funding institutions, competing for the two rotating Council seats, and maneuvering against each other in ways that would be exhausting if the Umbra wasn't also trying to kill everyone.

The Old Houses

Pre-Apostasy lineages. They were noble before the world ended.

House Aerincorvus

Motto: "Between two worlds, we are the door."

Seat: The Overgrown Palazzo, Medsen

Heraldry: A crow on silver ivy; deep forest black and iridescent green.

The Vale's only noble house of established Elven-Human lineage, Aerincorvus balances Medsen court politics with deep ties to druidic communities and Fae researchers. Their defining project is the Concordance — a massive archive documenting Fae-contact anomalies throughout the Vale. They believe the Faewilds were sealed, not destroyed, during the Apostasy, and they are quietly compiling evidence to prove it and force the Council to treat Fae studies as a legitimate research priority.

Most of the Vale considers this folklore. Aerincorvus considers the Vale's opinion a data point.

Good for characters with Elven heritage, druidic connections, or interest in the Faewilds.

House Aurelian

Motto: "We remember the sky."

Seat: The Solarium, Medsen

Heraldry: A golden eagle above a half-submerged sun; pale gold and faded white.

Formerly the Armisian Empire's agricultural nobility, the Aurelians worship the sun as the practical source of all life — and grieve, quietly and perpetually, its absence. They manage the Vale's major seed vaults and experimental greenhouses, stubbornly cultivating crops to thrive under Beacon-light. Their warm alliance with the Caretakers and their funding of astronomical research with House Lugner make them one of the Council's most reliable conservative votes.

Their optimism is genuine, and it occasionally makes them easy to exploit.

Good for characters with religious convictions, agrarian backgrounds, or interest in what the world looked like before the veil closed.

House Iyengar

Motto: "In every tongue, one word: endure."

Seat: The Amber Court, Medsen

Heraldry: A crossed blade and quill over an open fist; amber and deep teal.

Half-orc by origin — descended from an ancient marriage between an Armisian noble and an Orcish Prince — the Iyengar are Brightvale's neutral arbitrators. They combine institutional governance with Orcish directness and a deep reverence for covenants. Their Paladins draw power from personal ideals rather than divine light, a theological independence the Caretakers find quietly offensive.

They want to become an official Council-chartered arbitration body. They also want formal legal recognition extended to Orcenfolk communities outside Medsen. They have wanted both for a long time.

Good for characters with diplomatic, legal, or Orcish heritage; Paladins who draw on personal conviction.

House Kaewdyn

Motto: "The blood remembers what the mind forgets."

Seat: The Ashen Hall, Medsen

Heraldry: A silver lion holding a pale dragon's scale; deep charcoal and bone-white.

Kaewdyn carries draconic resonance from an ancient union with the extinct House Rjioha. Their "Ashen-Heirs" share a striking pale physiology and can physically sense the Umbra's malignant resonance — a gift that comes with a heavy psychological toll. Mandatory service in the Emberguard precedes any Kaewdyn claim to leadership.

They are warriors, not politicians. Medsen court life bores them. Their ambition is to officially merge the House into the Emberguard's highest command, which Lord Commander Varis Lugner supports in principle and Medsen's aristocracy opposes in practice.

Good for characters with draconic or martial heritage, or those who want an instinctive connection to the Umbra's presence.

House Lugner

Motto: "Truth is buried. We dig."

Seat: The Pale Sanctum, Medsen

Heraldry: A lidded eye over a burning candle; white and ash-grey.

Brightvale's strictest intellectual force — and one of its most controversial. Pre-dating the Apostasy, House Lugner was a lineage of magisters and deep-weave scholars. When the Apostasy fell, their ancestral matriarch struck a forbidden pact with a Void-Binder to preserve their arcane legacy. The consequence: many Lugner descendants are born as Infernis Tieflings, bearing the "Azure Stain" of gray-blue skin and dark horns.

They fund the Old Magic faction at the Academy and believe, passionately, that recovering the pre-Apostasy Deep-Weaves is the only path to real survival. Their most famous member, Lord Commander Varis Lugner, abandoned his arcane studies to command the Emberguard. The House has not forgiven him.

Good for Infernis characters, scholarly types, or those interested in pre-Apostasy magical history.

House Von Zoltraak

Motto: "The old lamp lit the road to the cliff. We build a new one."

Seat: The Crucible, Aurore mid-tier

Heraldry: A flame in an open hand; deep violet and burnished copper.

The progressive counterweight to House Lugner. The Von Zoltraaks are unsentimental about their Armisian lineage and blunt about their conclusions: Old Magic failed. The Apostasy proves it. The future lies in new arcane forms engineered specifically to fight the current Umbra reality — not in resurrecting what already failed once.

They fund the Progressive Aetherweaving faction at the Academy and maintain the Crucible's independent labs. Their greatest ambition: engineer a portable, non-Beacon-dependent Umbra-suppression field. Their strategist Drago Von Zoltraak was publicly sacrificed to the Beacon by Queen Wendreda after the Brightblood War, despite having fought for the Reprieve at Three Bridges. A portrait of Drago hangs in the Crucible's central hall, facing the door.

Good for progressive mages, engineers, or characters motivated by practical survival over historical reverence.

The Recent Houses

Post-Apostasy elevations. They earned their titles in the new world, not the old one.

House Ashwood

Motto: "The grove outlasts the storm."

Seat: The Greenmantle Lodge, Northern Plateau edge

Heraldry: A great oak with extending roots; deep forest green and earthy brown.

Elevated from common foresters who defended vital wilderness from the Umbra after the Apostasy, Ashwood is Brightvale's steadfast ecological advocate. They maintain critical timber reserves and supply the Lumen-infused wood the Academy depends on — leverage they manage carefully. Their ongoing battle to enshrine a permanent Forested Reserve into Council law has been their primary political project for three consecutive Council cycles.

Progress is slow. The trees, at least, are patient.

Good for rangers, druids, characters with roots in the common people, or those motivated by conservation.

House Drevorn

Motto: "What is held cannot be taken."

Seat: The Ironweight Vault, Medsen

Heraldry: A closed fist gripping scales; deep burgundy and grey.

The Drevorns did not fight their way to nobility, nor were they elevated for bloodline. They out-logisticed the old elite during the Apostasy crisis — storing grain, extending credit, managing supply lines when the Old Houses were busy losing a war — and never stopped. Today they control critical physical assets, trade routes, and a ledger of noble debt so extensive that half the Vale's aristocracy owes them money.

They are widely resented. Patriarch Corvin Drevorn openly intends to secure a permanent Council seat within his lifetime, and he has twenty years of accumulated favors to spend on it. The Old Houses hate that he might succeed.

Good for merchant backgrounds, information brokers, or characters navigating Medsen's political underworld.

House Kaze

Motto: (None recorded)

Seat: Multiple relay stations; administrative office in Medsen

Ancestry: Predominantly Orcenfolk

Kaze rose to nobility through an absolute monopoly on speed. They own and operate Brightvale's horse relay system — and in a world where horses are extraordinarily rare, this means they own the fastest communication network in the Vale. A message travels the 30 kilometers from Emberfort to Medsen in under four hours. In a world where delayed military reports can mean an Umbra breach, this makes them indispensable to both the Council and the Emberguard.

The Kaze know exactly what that indispensability is worth.

Good for Orcish characters, messengers, spies, or those with connections to the Vale's transportation networks.

House Ravenna

Motto: "Every road leads somewhere. We know where."

Seat: The Wayhouse, Medsen courier district

Heraldry: A crow in flight over a forked road; charcoal and slate blue.

Elevated from scouts who mapped Brightvale's first stable routes during the Apostasy, House Ravenna runs the definitive courier and intelligence network of the Vale. Their impeccable courier service doubles as an information operation. No one lies in a Ravenna post, because Ravenna clerks recognize inconsistencies.

Their ambition: legitimize what they already are. Transmute their private courier service into a state-funded, Council-protected intelligence body. Every major faction has considered what that would mean for their own secrets. Most have concluded it would not be ideal.

Grand Explorer Mira Ravenna shares the House name and operates with them intricately.

Good for rogues, information traders, scouts, or characters with shadowy institutional connections.

House Thalum

Motto: "The mountain holds. So shall we."

Seat: The Marrow Hall, Medsen's lower plateau

Heraldry: A pickaxe and mason's level crossed; slate grey and iron brown.

Note: Engineering lineage pre-dating the Apostasy; elevated formally after it.

House Thalum built Brightvale before the Apostasy struck. Literally: their engineering corps designed and constructed the plateau's walls, fortifications, and infrastructure. They maintain them still, and they are perpetually frustrated by politicians who defer crucial maintenance until structures fail. Their ongoing rivalry with Hvergi's Dwarven mining community over quarrying rights has been running for generations without resolution.

They own the plateau's bedrock by right of first survey. They consider this a serious legal claim.

Good for engineers, soldiers, or characters from Medsen's working class with little patience for aristocratic theater.

The Extinct Houses

They did not survive. Their stories explain why.

House Rjioha

Status: Extinct — Armisian High Nobility

Heraldry: A ship's prow cresting a wave with a star compass; deep sea-blue and silver.

Once the Armisian Empire's seafaring arm — responsible for intercontinental exploration, diplomacy, and trade. Their entire fleet was caught at sea when the Apostasy struck. Not a single vessel returned. The house was wiped from existence in hours.

Their genetics survive in House Kaewdyn through an ancestral marriage, which is the source of the Ashen-Heirs' draconic resonance. Modern Explorers maintain a small shrine to House Rjioha at Emberfort, considering them the patron saints of the lost expedition.

House Volex

Status: Extinct — Armisian High Nobility

Heraldry: A dragon rampant with spread wings; crimson and black.

The military linchpin of the Armisian Empire, Volex held a biological bond with war-dragons. They were the first house to fall in the Apostasy — not to the Umbra directly, but to a mysterious biological breakdown of their draconic bond. As the bond failed, the dragons mutated and Hollowed, bringing the Volex riders down with them.

Their last physical legacy: the Aetherweaver Academy's secured vaults hold the final confirmed surviving dragon eggs in stasis, their viability and potential Umbra-taint unknown. Whether the breakdown of the draconic bond was the first symptom of the Apostasy — or one of its causes — is a question scholars have argued about for four centuries.

Ancestries & Cultures

The Enduring are not one people. They were many peoples before the Apostasy, and they remain many now — crowded onto a single plateau, sharing a single Beacon, finding reasons to cooperate and reasons to argue with equal consistency.

Humankind

Heirs of the Armisian Empire

The most numerous ancestry in Brightvale. Humans carry the weight of the Armisian Empire in everything: their architecture, their legal systems, their social hierarchies, and their tendency to organize everything into Noble Houses whether the situation requires it or not.

Their short lifespans — compared to Elves and Dwarves — produce a distinctive urgency. Humans who want to achieve things achieve them in decades or not at all, which drives both remarkable ingenuity and remarkable impatience. The Aetherweaver Academy's structured magic was adopted so quickly by human mages largely because it was efficient — teachable in years rather than centuries.

Human culture in Brightvale is preoccupied with lineage and status. Who your ancestors were, which Houses they served or founded, what their name meant in the courts of Medsen — these things matter intensely to humans of the upper tiers and considerably less to those below, who have more immediate concerns.

Magic

Before Elven scholarship reached Brightvale, human magic operated on no framework at all — only belief. A human who needed fire had no theory of combustion. They simply needed fire with enough conviction that reality provided it. Faith moved flame. Grief split stone. This unstructured tradition produced effects that modern formulaic magic still cannot fully replicate. The Dawnfather's creation of the Beacon is the supreme example: a feat so far outside any known arcane framework that scholars who reverse-engineer it consistently reach dead ends.

Modern human mages use the Arcanum — a formulaic approach borrowed and adapted from Elven principles. Efficient, precise, teachable, and subject to the same hazard as the Elven tradition: Arcane Locks, self-imposed logical frameworks that can cage a mage's ceiling rather than raise it.

Naming Traditions

Noble and scholarly names (Central European in feel):

Kaleb, Florian, Lucien, Petyr, Matthias, Reinhardt, Harald, Narcissa, Liana, Lilianne, Aelfred, Florenz, Essek, Eldris, Wyll.

Common names:

Azi, Nayar, Thyazi, Thalia, Shadia, Kari, Neera.

Elves (Faefolk)

Children of the Severed Threshold

Before the Apostasy, Elves maintained a connection to the Faewilds — a parallel realm of ancient natural power. The Apostasy severed that connection. The Faewilds went quiet. The Fae stopped coming. What exactly happened is a wound the Elves have not finished processing four centuries later.

Elven philosophy in the Vale has fractured along three broad paths:

The Seekers believe the connection can be restored. They study Aetherweaving at Aurore's Peak, maintain the old megaliths and standing stones, and work with researchers like House Aerincorvus to document Fae-contact anomalies. The Faewilds were sealed, they insist. Not destroyed.

The Scholars believe the answers lie in the ruins of the old world. The Apostasy is the mystery worth solving, and solving it requires archaeology, archivism, and patience measured in centuries.

The Urban Elves have detached from the past and built their lives in Medsen or within the Noble Houses. Forward-looking, integrated, and occasionally regarded with quiet judgment by the other two groups.

Elves live considerably longer than humans, and this shows in how they approach everything. Their magical tradition is built on thorough understanding — the Formulaic Tradition, where a spell is an inevitable conclusion of correct reasoning rather than an act of will. The precision this produces is remarkable. The hazard is the Arcane Lock: a mage who has built a perfectly consistent internal framework may find themselves unable to advance past it, not from lack of power, but because their own reasoning has ruled out the next step. Breaking a Lock typically requires recognizing it is self-imposed — and then breaking the logic entirely, at least momentarily.

Home settlement: Many Elves live in Aeldenbarrow, a druidic enclave half-concealed by glamours near the Vale's western edge. Others are dispersed throughout Medsen, Aurore, and beyond.

Naming Traditions

Celtic in sound:

Cillian, Ciara, Eira, Maeve, Aodhán, Faolan, Fíadh, Elowen, Enriel, Cirdan, Hwynfer, Taliesin.

Dwarvenkind

The Rune-Keepers

Dwarven culture in Brightvale is built around a single conviction: this is not home. The Dwarves arrived on the Armisian coastline less than a century before the Apostasy — recent enough that the first generation to settle had made the crossing themselves. They knew where they had come from. They had names for the headlands. They remembered the smell of the water.

Then the Apostasy fell, the world ended, and the march north severed them from every coast entirely. Brightvale is landlocked. The Great Sea they remember is not myth. It is a place. It simply cannot be reached from here.

The Dwarves hold the Vale as a shore to defend until the Umbra recedes enough for the passage to become possible again — and they hold it with the same stubborn, sustained competence they brought to every shore before it.

Hvergi

The Dwarven enclave of Hvergi is carved into the eastern mountain-roots of Brightvale — mine, fortress, and cultural heartland in equal measure, founded in the first decades after the Apostasy. The Dwarves mine the deep crystal seams beneath the mountains: crystals used by Aetherweavers to focus the Beacon's light, some carrying latent magical energy of their own. This gives Hvergi a quiet but significant hold on Brightvale's arcane supply chain. They are aware of this. They manage it carefully.

Three ruling families govern Hvergi and have done so since its founding:

Clan Brumdain are the eldest family and the deepest miners — scholars of the mountain's grain, keepers of the oldest rune-stones. Their authority is geological as much as political.

Clan Hjalrim are Hvergi's warriors and gatekeepers, and the finest weaponsmiths in all of Brightvale. They decide who enters the enclave and, by extension, who matters.

Clan Sigr manage Hvergi's trade relationships with the outside world — the family most fluent in Medsen's political language, and the most controversial within the enclave for it.

The Hjalrim Blade

A Hjalrim blade is not a weapon. It is an inheritance.

Clan Hjalrim works Hvergi crystal shards directly into the steel during the smelt, producing blades that carry the crystal's natural resonance. In the darkness of the Wastes, a Hjalrim blade glows faintly — a pale blue-white light that unsettles Umbra-touched creatures. When the blade is further treated with ashgeld, the glow becomes something more: the blade burns in the dark, and Umbra-touched flesh does not tolerate it. Venturers who carry one describe the experience as fighting with a torch that also cuts.

There are perhaps one hundred such blades in existence across all of Brightvale. Each has a name. Clan Hjalrim does not sell them — they are gifted, rarely, to those the Clan considers worthy, and each one is tracked. If you meet a Dwarf who wants to know how a particular blade ended up in a particular hand, that is why.

Heimsfar

Every Dwarf in Hvergi knows the word Heimsfar — the Homeward Voyage. The prophecy holds that one day the Dwarven people will reach open water, build great ships, and sail back to the homeland from which the Apostasy cut them off. The earliest carvings of it were specific — coastal landmarks, sea-routes, distances. Four centuries of re-carving from slightly worn originals have reduced those specifics to symbol and impression: ships on dark water, fire on the horizon, a shore that is not this shore.

Whether the prophecy is a literal sailing plan that has been slowly corrupted into poetry, or always was poetry, is a question Dwarves argue about and never resolve. What is not argued: Brightvale is a shore to be held, not a home to be kept. The sea is still out there. The Dwarves will reach it.

A Dwarven character who cares about Heimsfar is not naive or backward-looking. They are carrying the longest patience in Brightvale — the conviction that survival now is in service of something larger, and that the work matters even if the destination is still beyond the horizon.

Naming Traditions

Norse in sound:

Storvald, Hjalrim, Merlos, Brumdain, Dain, Thormor, Tyr, Gyrid, Brigitte, Dyanna, Freyr, Eivor, Sigr.

Halflings

Guardians of Joy

Halflings hold the Halfling Hearthlands — the most important piece of real estate in Brightvale after Medsen itself. The agricultural heart of the valley. Their fields produce the majority of the Vale's food through communal agrarian ritual that blends practical farming with storytelling they believe keeps the lingering presence of the Fae woven into the soil. Whether this is mythology or mechanics, the Hearthlands produce harvests that Beacon-ash fertilizer alone does not explain.

Like Elves, Halflings retain a connection to the natural world that echoes their Fae-adjacent ancestry. They are not political in the way humans and Dwarves are political. They are concerned with different things: community, memory, the stories that bind people together, and the practice of joy as maintenance rather than luxury — something that requires active tending, especially in dark times.

Note: Some scholars consider Halflings a distinct branch of Faefolk ancestry. Halflings find this debate largely uninteresting.

Naming Traditions

Halflings tend toward warm, comfortable-sounding names — often with a rustic or Old English feel.

Examples: Rosie, Bramble, Tobias, Merric, Calla, Fen, Aldric, Petal, Oswin, Brix.

Orcenfolk

The Nomadic Senshi

Orcish culture blends the traditions of nomadic steppe peoples with the disciplined philosophy of a warrior class that treats combat as craft and craft as identity. In Brightvale, horses are extraordinarily rare — only a small number survived the trek up the Venturer's Trail, and the Brightblood War further devastated the population. The Orcish community are their stewards, handling the surviving bloodlines with the care reserved for things that cannot be replaced.

Through House Kaze, they operate the Vale's vital horse messenger relay. In battle, they station near Emberfort. The Verse of the Blade — the warrior philosophy that now dominates Slayer culture — originates in Orcish tradition: a combat philosophy that treats martial skill as inseparable from artistic expression, and holds that a warrior who fights without soul is no better than the things in the Wastes.

Orcish clans maintain significant autonomy outside Medsen's direct governance. House Iyengar has been pushing for formal legal recognition of non-Medsen Orcish communities for decades. Progress has been slow, but it has been made.

Naming Traditions

Japanese and Korean in sound:

Musha, Ryuujin, Orochi, Kasai, Kenshi, Haru, Rin, Hana, Hama, Goro, Goryo, Sakae, Nari, Jin, Nantai.

Infernis (Tieflings)

The Shard-Kin

The Infernis did not exist before the Apostasy. They are its children — the consequence of desperate bargains struck in the cataclysm's darkest years.

When the Umbra consumed civilization and survival looked like a matter of hours, various noble lineages and desperate individuals made pacts with extraplanar entities: Devils, Demons, beings from beyond the fraying fabric of a collapsing world. They survived. Their descendants bear the mark of those bargains in their blood, passed down through every generation since, permanent and indelible.

The physical form of an Infernis reveals the nature of the original pact:

Red-skinned Infernis descend from diabolical pacts — lineages associated with themes of order, contracts, and rigid hierarchy.

Gray or blue-skinned Infernis descend from demonic pacts — lineages associated with raw power, primal resonance, and the chaotic survivalism of the Apostasy's worst hours. House Lugner carries this phenotype most prominently, which they regard as a feature.

Despite — or because of — their unusual origin, the Infernis are not outcasts in Brightvale. They are visible reminders that the people of the Vale did whatever they had to do to survive. Many find that admirable in retrospect. High-ranking Caretakers who devote their lives to the Beacon sometimes adopt Latinate names to mark their dedication.

Magic

The extraplanar entities of the original pacts are gone — vanished along with the gods. What remains is the bloodline and the Warlock tradition it carries: magic through obsessive specialization. Where Elven magic builds universal frameworks and human magic reaches for raw faith, Warlock magic picks one domain and pursues it until the distinction between knowing something and being able to do it collapses entirely. A Warlock who has spent decades mastering movement eventually stops asking how to move through air and begins asking why they couldn't. Flight becomes not a feat but an absence of assumption.

Infernis practitioners do not universally follow this path — but those who do often find it comes more naturally to them than to practitioners of any other ancestry.

Naming Traditions

Infernis generally follow Human naming conventions. Those with deep Caretaker devotion sometimes adopt Latinate names:

Dante, Maximus, Beatrice, Gabriel, Vergil, Lucia, Augustus, Lucian, Cassius, Sylvia, Orpheus.

Rumours & Whispers

A Compendium of What People Are Saying

Collected from the common rooms of Emberfort's Guild-Hall, the courier posts of the Wayhouse, the less reputable establishments of Medsen's lower tiers, and one very talkative merchant outside the Halfling Hearthlands who refused to say how he knew any of it.

Accuracy is not guaranteed. Interestingness is.

Within Brightvale

"The King hasn't been seen in seven years. Seven. Nobody's that busy with paperwork."

King Alfwyn retreated into the Central Temple-Castle shortly after his coronation and stopped all public appearances. The High Steward speaks for the crown. The theories range from illness to something he witnessed inside the Beacon's core that broke him entirely. Nobody has disproven any of them because nobody has been allowed close enough to try.

"House Aurelian's new wheat glows in the dark."

A wheat variety grown in the Aurelian experimental greenhouses photosynthesizes off the Beacon's light — and at night, it glows faintly blue. The Caretakers have dispatched observers to the greenhouses. They have not yet explained to House Aurelian what they're looking for.

"There's a sealed courier package sitting in the Wayhouse with no pickup. Six months, enormous bounty, anonymous sender. The recipient hasn't been seen since winter."

House Ravenna's clerks are professionally obligated not to discuss their clients. The fact that they haven't opened the package themselves suggests either impeccable ethics or genuine fear of what's inside.

"Corvin Drevorn is hiring. Very quietly. Someone stole a ledger from the Ironweight Vault and he needs it back before whoever has it figures out what's written in it."

The ledger allegedly contains the names and specific blackmail material for approximately half the Vale's nobility. Drevorn is willing to pay a considerable sum to avoid finding out who they'll sell it to, and to whom.

"The Thalum engineers have flagged a structural failure in Emberfort's eastern wall. Four separate reports in two years. The Council keeps deferring the vote on repairs."

The Thalum engineers' estimates on when the wall might fail without intervention vary depending on which engineer you ask. None of the estimates are comfortable.

"There's something moving through Medsen's lower tiers at night. Looks human. Drains people."

Caretaker healers have noted a pattern: patients presenting with extreme vitality loss, no visible wounds, and no memory of the previous night. The official position is Umbra-adjacent illness. The pattern doesn't match anything in the standard Umbra exposure literature.

"An Iyengar Paladin is being quietly tried by the Caretakers' tribunal for channeling divine power 'outside orthodox sources.' The Paladin says she's always drawn on personal conviction, not the Beacon. The Caretakers say that's precisely the problem."

The trial hasn't been made public. It has become public anyway, through the fastest information network in the Vale: people talking about it in the market at three different stalls simultaneously.

"House Aerincorvus had an investigator go missing. She was documenting a glade where 'the air tasted wrong.' That's all the last report said."

The Aerincorvus Concordance has catalogued eleven sites in the Vale's western edge with similar descriptions. The missing investigator had developed a theory connecting them. The theory is presumably in her notes. The notes are with her, wherever she is.

"Someone has been attending open lectures at the Academy who doesn't appear on any registry. Asks extremely precise questions about Umbra containment. Registers magically as 'not present.'"

The Academy's administrative staff have confirmed this three separate times. The Tower's Arch-Aetherweavers are aware. They have not publicly acted on this information, which is itself information worth noting.

"The Hvergi Dwarves stopped submitting quarterly mineral yield reports six weeks ago. House Thalum filed a formal inquiry. The Dwarves haven't responded."

This is unusual — Hvergi bureaucracy is meticulous to the point of tedium. House Thalum suspects they struck something in the deep seams they don't want to share. Hvergi suspects that if they do share it, Thalum will use the information to justify a territorial claim. Both suspicions are probably correct.

"The yearly tournaments are coming. Three houses have already submitted challengers for the Blade-Ring. There's an unofficial betting pool on whether the Slayer's Pit champion will enter."

The tournaments are equal parts genuine competition and barely veiled political theater. The betting is enthusiastic, the odds are calculated by people who know more than they should, and First Slayer Makjar has neither confirmed nor denied the rumor of her participation.

"House Von Zoltraak built a portable Umbra suppression device. It works. The failure mode is that it rebounds the Umbra at double density into the containment zone."

The device has not been submitted for Council review. House Von Zoltraak maintains it needs more testing. People who have heard about the failure mode agree with this assessment.

"A cult in the lower city is trying to bring back a vampire lord's lover. The vampire lord in question is reportedly still alive — or something like alive — and is funding the operation."

The Caretakers have categorically denied the existence of vampires in Brightvale. They have denied it with some specificity, which is considered suspicious by people who have noticed these things.

Outside Brightvale — The Wastes

"There's a city out there. Six, maybe seven days south. Empty — no Umbra-touched inside its walls. Nothing inside its walls at all."

First reported by Venturers in 395 AA. Multiple subsequent expeditions have confirmed the city exists. None have found an explanation for why the Umbra-touched avoid it entirely. The Explorers' Guild has classified this as a Priority Site. An investigation is being assembled.

"Someone came back from the Wastes talking about a lost Armisian legion. Still at their posts. Silver armor, weapons that glow. Waiting for orders that will never come."

The Venturers who filed this report were coherent, unHollowed, and consistent in their testimony. The Explorers' Guild categorized it as "unconfirmed but serious." The Slayers filed it under "things that will eventually require our attention."

"The Southern Quake opened up something beneath the plateau. Explorers are calling it the Chasm — a massive underground complex, multiple entrances, no map of the interior. Whatever's down there has been down there a long time."

The Academy has dispatched scholars to the entrance points. The Explorers' Guild has dispatched Venturers. The Caretakers have asked both parties to report anything that looks like a shrine. Nobody has asked the Caretakers why.

"Kaewdyn scouts are reporting their Umbra-sensitivity triggering at levels that don't match any threat they can identify. Their commander says the signal feels 'structured.' Not chaotic. Structured."

House Kaewdyn's military hierarchy is taking this seriously. The Slayers, when asked, said that a structured signal would imply coordination at a level that should not be possible. They did not elaborate. They looked like people who had elaborated on this topic privately and found it unpleasant.

"The Frost-Veil Pass leads somewhere. Explorers found a route through the northern peaks twelve years ago. There are Elven ruins beyond the ice deserts. Nobody has come back with a complete picture of what's there."

The Guild maintains this as a Technical Route — available to elite parties, not standard expeditions. What built the ruins, when, and why they're in the frozen north are unanswered questions. Elf scholars at Aeldenbarrow have declined to speculate publicly.

"Grand Explorer Mira Ravenna has been quietly suppressing certain route maps. Removing them from the master cartography after they come in. The Venturers who filed the originals have noticed."

House Ravenna filed an intelligence report on this. The Grand Explorer hasn't moved against the source of the leak. The suppressed routes all lead toward the same general region of the southern Wastes. Nobody who has asked the Grand Explorer directly about this has received a direct answer.

"There are dragon eggs in the Wastes. Wild ones — not the clutch in the Academy vaults. Found in the deep southern ruins. Nobody knows if they're viable."

Multiple independent Venturing parties have reported fragments consistent with dragon egg casings. The Academy is very interested. The Slayers are interested in a different way. Nobody's definition of "viable" is the same.

"Some of the ruins in the deep Wastes don't match Armisian architecture. Or any architecture anyone can identify. They were built before the Empire. The question is by what — and where did they go?"

The Academy's research archives have been compiling this data for thirty years. The patterns suggest at least two prior civilizations, both of which ended in ways that rhyme uncomfortably with the Apostasy.

"The Umbra-touched aren't just expanding — they're organizing differently. Arch-Revenants coordinating in ways Slayer veterans say they haven't seen before. Covering flanks. Adjusting to counter-tactics."

Three independent Slayer field reports in the last year. First Slayer Makjar has reviewed all of them personally and has made no public statement. The Slayers who filed the reports are still on active duty. The Guild is watching this carefully enough that the watching is itself becoming visible.

"A Venturing party came back reporting a working settlement in the Wastes. Lights. Smoke. No contact made. The Explorers' Guild is not authorized to confirm or deny whether this has been verified."

Filed by a single party. Not dismissed. The Grand Explorer did not laugh when the report was presented, which is considered significant by everyone who was in the room.
